tests/unit/test_cli.py:23-25 carries the claim and defines _MYSQL_URL = "mysql+pymysql://u@db.invalid/shop". RFC 6761 section 6.4 says users may assume .invalid names always return NXDOMAIN. It says resolution libraries and caching resolvers SHOULD return an immediate negative response, so a conforming resolver does not resolve db.invalid. Every DB URL in the file that can reach a connect uses the .invalid host. These are _MYSQL_URL (the _write_serve_config default at :47 and _build_cfg at :817) and the inline TOML urls at :356, :431, :640, :905 and :1019. :291 asserts the fake connect received host == "db.invalid". The autouse mysql_connect fixture (:28) also fakes pymysql.connect. Counterexample traced: a hosts-file entry or a search-domain wildcard such as db.invalid.corp.example. A hosts entry is a deliberate local override, and a resolver that honours it for .invalid does not follow the RFC's SHOULD. A search-list suffix only matters if the resolver expands it, which the 'conforming resolver' qualifier excludes. Neither is an input a shipped caller produces. The claim's qualifier ('conforming resolver') is accurate and not overstated. The rejection line in `rejections` is about test_safety.py and does not cover this item.

tests/integration/conftest.py:39-41 comment says '.invalid' does not resolve 'under a conforming resolver' and MYSQL_URL = 'mysql+pymysql://u@db.invalid/shop' (host db.invalid). RFC 6761 section 6.4 (the stated source of truth) reserves 'invalid.' so that name resolution APIs/libraries SHOULD recognize it and return an immediate negative (NXDOMAIN) response, and users may assume such queries always return NXDOMAIN. The claim is explicitly scoped to a conforming resolver, so it is the RFC property restated. Absolute-claim trace: the input that would break it is a hosts-file entry '127.0.0.1 db.invalid' (or a wildcard DNS record under a resolver search-domain suffix, which glibc tries after NXDOMAIN of the as-is name since db.invalid has 1 dot). A resolver that honors the hosts entry for an .invalid name is exactly one that departs from the 6.4 recommendation, so it is outside the claim's 'conforming' scope; the search-suffix case queries a different name (db.invalid.<suffix>), not the reserved name, and requires an unusual wildcard DNS setup. Neither is produced by any shipped code; the unit/integration fixtures use db.invalid only as a never-connected placeholder (conftest.py:4-8 says the DB is never connected to). The rejections line concerns an unrelated safety test and does not cover this item. Residual caveat: the wording is slightly stronger than reality on non-conforming local configs, a comment-only concern.
